learning_objective: The learner will assess six citations for the same claim by marking exactly which of four quality criteria each fails, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** citation-quality-checker
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** assess
**Learning Objective:** The learner will assess six citations for the same claim by marking exactly which of four quality criteria each fails, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Citation Quality, Source Citation, Primary Source, Secondary Source (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each citation the learner marks the failed criteria, or marks none. A judgment is correct when the marked set equals the Failed criteria column in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A citation with a link is always good. (2) A recent source is always reliable. (3) A source that exists supports the claim. **Instructional Rationale:** Assessing a citation against explicit criteria is an Evaluate-level action. Six citations for one claim, with different mixes of failures, force the learner to apply each criterion separately. **Content:** The claim shown at all times: "Lake Marlow's deepest point is 31 meters." The four criteria: Relevant, Reliable, Retrievable, Current. A criterion is met when: the source states the depth (Relevant); the author or publisher is an agency, a reviewed publication, or a reference work with a stated method (Reliable); the link works or full details let a reader find the source (Retrievable); and the source is dated within the last five years (Current). The six citations (all made up): | # | Citation shown to the learner | Failed criteria | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 2025. https://example.gov/lake-marlow (link works, and the sheet gives the depth) | None | It states the depth, comes from an agency, can be opened, and is recent. | | 2 | A blog post titled "Why I Love Lakes," 2019, no link, which never mentions depth | Relevant, Reliable, Retrievable | The post does not state the depth, has no stated method, and cannot be found. | | 3 | State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 1998. https://example.gov/lake-marlow-1998 (link works, and the sheet gives the depth) | Current | The source is old for a measurement that can be resurveyed. | | 4 | State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 2025. https://example.gov/old-link (the link returns "page not found") | Retrievable | The source may be good, and the reader cannot reach it. | | 5 | A student slide deck about lakes, 2025, no author, no link, which states the depth | Reliable, Retrievable | The deck states the depth, and no one is accountable for it and no one can find it. | | 6 | State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Survey." 2025. https://example.gov/marlow-survey (link works, and the survey reports area and shoreline length but not depth) | Relevant | The source is reliable and current, and it does not address depth. | **Provenance:** The claim and citations are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The criteria follow the chapter section "Citation Quality". The five-year limit for Current is a teaching choice, and the sim labels it "illustrative threshold". **Rules:** Each citation has a fixed set of failed criteria, and the empty set is valid. A citation is Current when it is dated >= 2021, because the sim's review date is 2026. The criteria are judged independently. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees the claim, the four criteria, and one citation. 2. The learner marks each criterion that the citation fails, or marks "None fail". 3. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the correct set and the Why text. 4. The learner moves to the next citation, until citation 6 is done. **Feedback:** 6 citations in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. Failed: [criteria, or none]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can judge a citation." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed citation. **Starting State:** The claim, the four criteria with their definitions, and citation 1 with no criteria marked. The question shown is "Which criteria does this citation fail?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists the four citation-quality questions as relevant, reliable, retrievable, and current. The chapter says a citation that exists can fail to support the claim.
